explanations.explanation: Right there in the back, friend. The text says David and his men marched behind the Philistine leaders with Achish (1 Samuel 29:2). Achish, king of Gath, is the one walking with them (1 Samuel 27:2). I think that spot in line is exactly why the commanders start squinting at them.

Not out front, friend. The text puts David and his men marching behind the leaders with Achish (1 Samuel 29:2). The front was for the Philistine leaders with their units of hundreds and thousands. David's crew was tucked in the back like the last cookie on the cooling rack.

They're in the back, so I see why you went there. But the text doesn't say anything about supplies. It says David and his men marched behind the leaders with Achish (1 Samuel 29:2). Back of the line, yes. Supply duty, never mentioned.

True, and Achish is not shy about it. He says David has been with him all these days, even years, and "…from the day he defected until today I have found no fault in him." (1 Samuel 29:3) That's a glowing review from a king. As far as Achish is concerned, David's work history with him is spotless.

Actually it's true. Achish says, "…from the day he defected until today I have found no fault in him." (1 Samuel 29:3) He's standing up for David in front of his own commanders. Achish is writing David a reference letter right there in the line.

explanations.answer: Send him back where you assigned him
explanations.explanation: That's it. The commanders tell Achish, "Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him." (1 Samuel 29:4) They want David out of the battle line, and they say it plain. No committee, no vote, just "send him home."

explanations.answer: Hand him over to King Saul
explanations.explanation: Nope, nothing about handing David to Saul, king of Israel. The commanders say, "Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him." (1 Samuel 29:4) They want him sent back to his post. Handing him over would be a whole different plan.

explanations.answer: Keep him under guard in the camp
explanations.explanation: No guards in this one, friend. The commanders say, "Send that man back and let him return to the place you assigned him." (1 Samuel 29:4) They want him gone from the battle, not locked up in camp. Sending him back is the whole request.

Adversary, yes. The commanders say David "…must not go down with us into battle only to become our adversary during the war." (1 Samuel 29:4) An adversary is an opponent. They're worried he'll end up on the other side in the fight.

A protector is the opposite of what they're afraid of. They say David must not go into battle "…only to become our adversary during the war." (1 Samuel 29:4) They're picturing him turning on them. Nobody here is hoping for a bodyguard.

A messenger isn't the word, friend. The commanders say David must not become "…our adversary during the war." (1 Samuel 29:4) The worry they name is him becoming an adversary in the fight. Nothing in their words is about carrying messages.

explanations.answer: He has slain even more than Saul
explanations.explanation: That's the song. The commanders quote it: "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands…" (1 Samuel 29:5) In that tune, David gets tens of thousands and Saul gets thousands. It's a catchy song, and the Philistine commanders have clearly heard it.

explanations.answer: He is Saul's most loyal servant
explanations.explanation: The song isn't about loyalty, friend. It goes, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands…" (1 Samuel 29:5) It's a song about battle numbers, and David's number is bigger. The commanders use it as a warning.

explanations.answer: He is the bravest of the Philistines
explanations.explanation: David isn't a Philistine in that song. The words are, "Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands…" (1 Samuel 29:5) It compares David to Saul, king of Israel. The commanders bring it up when they tell Achish to send David back.

Close, but it's the other way around. Achish tells David, "But you are not good in the sight of the leaders." (1 Samuel 29:6) Achish thinks David is upright. The leaders don't agree. That's why David is getting sent back.

False is right. Achish says David has been upright in his own sight, then adds, "But you are not good in the sight of the leaders." (1 Samuel 29:6) He has to deliver the bad news to David's face. I bet that's not a fun talk to give.

Enemies, yes. David asks what Achish has found against him "…to keep me from going along to fight against the enemies of my lord the king?" (1 Samuel 29:8) He's asking to be let into the fight. That's his question.
Not servants, friend. David asks about fighting "…against the enemies of my lord the king?" (1 Samuel 29:8) The word is enemies, and that's the fight he says he wants to join.
Friends is a gentle word, but it's not here. David says he wants to fight "…against the enemies of my lord the king?" (1 Samuel 29:8) Nobody in that sentence is fighting friends. The word is enemies.
Early is right. Achish says to "…get up early in the morning…" (1 Samuel 29:10). It's an early start. I'd be hitting snooze on that one, and I've slept in a drawer.
Light is right. Achish says to go "…as soon as it is light." (1 Samuel 29:10) The orders are to leave once there's light. No lingering over breakfast.
Late would be a nice change, but no. Achish says to "…get up early in the morning…" (1 Samuel 29:10). The word is early. Sleeping in isn't on the schedule.

Dark is close to the time of day, but the word is light. Achish says to go "…as soon as it is light." (1 Samuel 29:10) The text says they get up early. The orders for leaving are about light, not dark.

Noon is way too late for these orders. Achish says to "…get up early in the morning…" and go "…as soon as it is light." (1 Samuel 29:10) The day starts early for David and his men. Noon is lunchtime for everybody else.

explanations.answer: Back to the land of the Philistines
explanations.explanation: That's the road. David and his men got up early "…to return to the land of the Philistines." (1 Samuel 29:11) Achish had told them to go in the morning (1 Samuel 29:10). Same direction the commanders asked for.

Bethlehem is a good guess, but that's not where they go. The text says they got up early "…to return to the land of the Philistines." (1 Samuel 29:11) They're headed back toward the land of the Philistines.

explanations.answer: Over to Saul's camp at Gilboa
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says David and his men got up early "…to return to the land of the Philistines." (1 Samuel 29:11) Saul is king of Israel, and Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel (1 Samuel 29:1). David's crew heads the other way.
True. The last line says, "And the Philistines went up to Jezreel." (1 Samuel 29:11) That's where Israel was camped by the spring (1 Samuel 29:1). David goes one way and the Philistines go another.

It's actually true, friend. The passage ends with, "And the Philistines went up to Jezreel." (1 Samuel 29:11) That's the same place Israel camped by the spring (1 Samuel 29:1). The Philistines are on the move.
